claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among the quinary and reduced-component FCC alloys originate from differences in chemical short-range ordering.
Greater chemical complexity in the quinary alloy produces a higher density of nanoscale ordered clusters than in the quaternary or ternary alloys.
Nanoscale SRO clusters locally distort the lattice.
SRO clusters impede dislocation motion more effectively in the quinary alloy than in the reduced-component alloys.
The compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys have been thermomechanically processed into single-phase FCC microstructures.
In-situ TEM mechanical testing can directly reveal dislocation behavior in these alloys.
High-resolution APT can quantify nanoscale SRO in these alloys.
The structural mediator is the presence and spatial distribution of nanoscale SRO clusters and their associated localized lattice distortions.
Increasing constituent count promotes formation of SRO clusters.
SRO clusters act as pinning sites for dislocations during deformation.
Greater dislocation pinning increases yield strength.
Greater dislocation pinning increases strain-hardening rate and alters failure mechanisms.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary alloy will have lower yield strength and strain-hardening rate and will exhibit intermediate mechanical properties.
The ternary alloy will show the least resistance to dislocation motion and the lowest yield strength.
In-situ TEM will reveal more pronounced dislocation pinning and lower dislocation mobility in the quinary alloy than in the simpler alloys.
APT will show a higher density or stronger clustering of ordered regions in the quinary alloy than in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy previously demonstrated distinct mechanical properties after identical processing.
The proposed comparison is applicable when second phases, porosity, and large-scale segregation are eliminated and loading conditions are identical at room temperature.
Direct detection and quantification of nanoscale SRO are technically challenging.
The correlation between SRO density and dislocation behavior is currently uncertain.
